variants.name: Typed closures over Sequence APIs
variants.implementation_notes: The everyday Swift form is a closure: `let overdue: (Invoice) -> Bool = { $0.daysPastDue >= 30 }`, composed by writing a new closure or a small combinator, and consumed by Sequence/Collection APIs (filter, allSatisfy, contains(where:), first(where:)) - no class hierarchy is needed. Foundation's Predicate/#Predicate is the modern library form when the same rule must also drive SwiftData or Core Data fetches, and it is covered as the sibling variant. A protocol-based Specification with isSatisfiedBy is justified mainly when rules are registered dynamically, must be logged by name, or are injected as dependencies; for local checks the closure is idiomatic and avoids one conformance per rule.
pitfalls: Closures capture reference types by reference: a rule that captures a mutable property or view model reads it at evaluation time, so the effective rule changes between calls - capture constants.
Storing heterogeneous rules in an array needs the explicit function type ((Invoice) -> Bool); inference fails for `let rules = [overdue, { $0.inCollection }]`.
Filtering an already-fetched array evaluates in memory; when the same rule must also drive a fetch it has to exist as a FetchDescriptor predicate, a second definition that can drift.
A throwing closure does not satisfy a non-throwing predicate parameter, so composed helpers must decide whether evaluation can fail.

variants.name: Foundation Predicate with the #Predicate macro
variants.idiom_name: Predicate<T> / #Predicate macro (SwiftData and Core Data fetch)
variants.implementation_notes: Foundation's Predicate<T> models the rule as an expression tree built by the #Predicate macro: the closure inside the macro is transformed at compile time into PredicateExpressions, boolean conditions compose with &&/||/!, Predicate.evaluate runs the rule in memory, and SwiftData/Core Data translate the same tree into SQL for FetchDescriptor/@Query - one rule for validation and fetching. The macro accepts only the operations it knows (no nested declarations, no flow control, a limited string API) and very dynamic composition can defeat the type checker, so the closure variant remains the general-purpose form and the predicate is the form to choose when the query side matters.
pitfalls: The macro only accepts a fixed operation set: nested declarations, flow control and many String methods are compile errors, so a rule that reads naturally as a closure may be impossible to express.

Dynamic composition of Predicate values is hard: the expression is type-erased behind `any StandardPredicateExpression`, and hand-built wrappers that satisfy evaluate may not be translatable by SwiftData (runtime unsupported-predicate errors).
Only constants in scope can be captured; external mutable state (Date.now, a mutable property) must be copied to a local before the macro, otherwise the predicate fails to compile or changes meaning.
Long chained conditions can overwhelm the type checker and stop compiling; split the rule into named sub-predicates combined outside the macro.
